<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-2"><span>a) Strong sustainability</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-2"><span>b) Weak sustainability</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-2"><span>c) The precautionary principle</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-2"><span>d) Sufficiency</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>Weak sustainability assumes that natural capital can in principle be substituted by manufactured or human capital, as long as total capital and total utility are maintained. </div>
<div class="webex-box quiz-question">
<p class="quiz-meta">Question 3.3 &middot; Based on section 3.1.2</p>
<p class="quiz-stem">In ecological economics, the economy draws energy and raw materials from the ecosystem (source function) and releases waste and emissions back into it. What is this second function called? (One word.)</p>

<p class="quiz-stem">From a neoclassical perspective, why are CO₂ emissions too high?</p>
<div class="webex-radiogroup" id="webex-q3-4" data-answer="[0, 1, 0, 0]">
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-4"><span>a) Because firms are not aware of climate change</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-4"><span>b) Because only private costs are reflected in the price, fossil-based goods are too cheap and the equilibrium quantity is too high</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-4"><span>c) Because markets are generally unable to coordinate production</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-4"><span>d) Because economic growth inevitably increases emissions</span></label>

<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>Climate change is a negative externality and therefore a market failure. </div>

<p class="quiz-stem">GDP grows by 3% per year, while CO₂ emissions grow by 1% per year. What is this called?</p>
<div class="webex-radiogroup" id="webex-q3-5" data-answer="[0, 1, 0, 0]">
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-5"><span>a) Absolute decoupling</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-5"><span>b) Relative decoupling</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-5"><span>c) A rebound effect</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-5"><span>d) No decoupling</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>Relative decoupling means emissions or resource use grow more slowly than GDP but still grow. Absolute decoupling of CO₂ can be observed in some countries of the Global North, but not at the global level, and not for resource consumption.</p></details>
</div>

<p class="quiz-stem">A household buys a fuel-efficient car and, because driving is now cheaper, drives longer distances. What is this an example of?</p>
<div class="webex-radiogroup" id="webex-q3-6" data-answer="[1, 0, 0, 0]">
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-6"><span>a) A direct rebound effect</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-6"><span>b) An indirect rebound effect</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-6"><span>c) Absolute decoupling</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-6"><span>d) The sufficiency strategy</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>A direct rebound effect occurs when efficiency gains make the same service cheaper and people use more of it. Rebound effects are why ecological economics sees efficiency as necessary but not sufficient.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="webex-box quiz-question">

<p class="quiz-stem">A policy makes some people better off by CHF 100 in total and others worse off by CHF 40 in total. The losers are not compensated. How do the two efficiency criteria judge this policy?</p>
<div class="webex-radiogroup" id="webex-q3-7" data-answer="[0, 1, 0, 0]">
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-7"><span>a) It is a Pareto improvement and meets the Kaldor-Hicks criterion</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-7"><span>b) It is not a Pareto improvement, but it meets the Kaldor-Hicks criterion</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-7"><span>c) It is a Pareto improvement, but it does not meet the Kaldor-Hicks criterion</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q3-7"><span>d) It meets neither criterion</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>A Pareto improvement requires that nobody is made worse off, which is not the case here. The Kaldor-Hicks criterion only requires that the winners could hypothetically compensate the losers and still be better off (100 &gt; 40), whether or not compensation actually happens. That is why the script says Kaldor-Hicks brings us back to the utilitarian view.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="webex-box quiz-question">

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
**Question 3.1** (based on section 3.1.1)

Which two planetary boundaries are considered core boundaries, because they combine the processes of many other subsystems?

a) Ocean acidification and aerosol loading
b) Climate change and biosphere integrity
c) Land-use change and freshwater use
d) Stratospheric ozone and novel entities

**Question 3.2** (based on section 3.1.2)

A government argues that extracting more oil is sustainable because the revenues are invested in schools and new technologies, so total capital is maintained. Which position does this reflect?

a) Strong sustainability
b) Weak sustainability
c) The precautionary principle
d) Sufficiency

**Question 3.3** (based on section 3.1.2)

In ecological economics, the economy draws energy and raw materials from the ecosystem (source function) and releases waste and emissions back into it. What is this second function called? (One word.)

Answer: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

**Question 3.4** (based on section 3.1.3)

From a neoclassical perspective, why are CO₂ emissions too high?

a) Because firms are not aware of climate change
b) Because only private costs are reflected in the price, fossil-based goods are too cheap and the equilibrium quantity is too high
c) Because markets are generally unable to coordinate production
d) Because economic growth inevitably increases emissions

**Question 3.5** (based on section 3.1.3)

GDP grows by 3% per year, while CO₂ emissions grow by 1% per year. What is this called?

a) Absolute decoupling
b) Relative decoupling
c) A rebound effect
d) No decoupling

**Question 3.6** (based on section 3.1.3)

A household buys a fuel-efficient car and, because driving is now cheaper, drives longer distances. What is this an example of?

a) A direct rebound effect
b) An indirect rebound effect
c) Absolute decoupling
d) The sufficiency strategy

**Question 3.7** (based on section 3.2.2)

A policy makes some people better off by CHF 100 in total and others worse off by CHF 40 in total. The losers are not compensated. How do the two efficiency criteria judge this policy?

a) It is a Pareto improvement and meets the Kaldor-Hicks criterion
b) It is not a Pareto improvement, but it meets the Kaldor-Hicks criterion
c) It is a Pareto improvement, but it does not meet the Kaldor-Hicks criterion
d) It meets neither criterion

**Question 3.8** (based on section 3.2.2)

According to John Rawls’s difference principle, when are social and economic inequalities acceptable?

a) When they result from free market exchange
b) When they maximize total utility in society
c) When they are to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, and positions are open to all under fair equality of opportunity
d) Never, because justice requires equal outcomes

**Question 3.9** (based on section 3.2.5)

According to the script, what is an important reason why the labour share of income has been falling in many countries?

a) Workers have become less productive
b) Power relations have shifted in favour of capital, because capital is highly mobile in an open world economy while labour is not
c) Wages have risen faster than profits since the 1980s
d) Most people now live from capital income

#### Answers and explanations {.unnumbered}

**3.1** b). Climate change and biosphere integrity act at a supraregional level and integrate many other subsystems. Reaching tipping points in these two systems can push the entire Earth system into a new state. According to the 2025 Planetary Health Check, seven of the nine boundaries have been crossed.

**3.2** b). Weak sustainability assumes that natural capital can in principle be substituted by manufactured or human capital, as long as total capital and total utility are maintained. This requires putting a monetary value on everything. Strong sustainability regards natural capital as only partly substitutable and relies on prevention rather than compensation.

**3.3** “sink” / “sink function”. The sink function. The economy is a subsystem of a finite global ecosystem and depends on both functions. Only solar energy enters the system from outside, while waste heat leaves it.

**3.4** b). Climate change is a negative externality and therefore a market failure. The social marginal costs lie above the private ones, so the market equilibrium (A) produces more than the social optimum (B), causing a welfare loss. The policy answer is to internalize the costs, for example with a CO₂ tax or emissions trading.

**3.5** b). Relative decoupling means emissions or resource use grow more slowly than GDP but still grow. Absolute decoupling would require emissions to fall while GDP grows. Absolute decoupling of CO₂ can be observed in some countries of the Global North, but not at the global level, and not for resource consumption.

**3.6** a). A direct rebound effect occurs when efficiency gains make the same service cheaper and people use more of it. If the household instead spent the savings on a holiday flight, that would be an indirect rebound effect. Rebound effects are why ecological economics sees efficiency as necessary but not sufficient.

**3.7** b). A Pareto improvement requires that nobody is made worse off, which is not the case here. The Kaldor-Hicks criterion only requires that the winners could hypothetically compensate the losers and still be better off (100 > 40), whether or not compensation actually happens. That is why the script says Kaldor-Hicks brings us back to the utilitarian view.

**3.8** c). Behind a “veil of ignorance”, people who do not know their own position or abilities would accept inequalities only under these two conditions. Option B is utilitarianism, which accepts inequality whenever total utility rises, regardless of distribution.

**3.9** b). Financial capital can move around the world in seconds, while borders, families and friendships keep workers in place. This weakened the post-war compromise between firms and trade unions. Technological change, including artificial intelligence, reinforces the trend. Until the 1970s, more than half of GDP was earned through labour; in the 2000s the share fell below 50% in most countries.

:::
